title: Body Language & Culture
subtitle: Greet, eat, and navigate everyday customs with confidence

lessons.title: La politesse française
lessons.description: Revise tu/vous, learn how the French greet each other, and use everyday polite formulas naturally.

blocks.heading: Tu or vous? A quick revision
blocks.body: "Tu" is for family, friends, children, and people your own age in informal settings. "Vous" is for strangers, older people, professional contexts, and anyone you want to show respect to. When in doubt, start with "vous" — the other person will usually invite you to switch with "On peut se tutoyer ?"

examples.french: Tu habites où ?
examples.english: Where do you live?

examples.french: Où habitez-vous ?
examples.english: Where do you live?

examples.english: Can we use "tu" with each other?

examples.english: I use "vous" with you out of respect.

examples.french: Entre collègues, on se tutoie parfois vite.
examples.english: Between colleagues, people sometimes switch to "tu" quickly.

blocks.tip: Age and hierarchy matter more than friendliness — a warm smile can still come with "vous".

blocks.heading: Greeting customs: la bise and the handshake
blocks.body: Among friends and family, French people often greet with "la bise" — light kisses on the cheek, usually two, though the number and side vary by region. In professional settings, a handshake is standard, especially for a first meeting.

examples.french: On se fait la bise ?
examples.english: Shall we do the cheek kisses?

examples.french: Elle m'a fait la bise en arrivant.
examples.english: She kissed my cheeks when she arrived.

examples.french: Il m'a serré la main fermement.

examples.french: Entre hommes, on se serre souvent la main.
examples.english: Between men, people often shake hands.

examples.french: Le nombre de bises change selon la région.
examples.english: The number of cheek kisses changes depending on the region.

blocks.tip: If you're unsure which greeting to use, let the other person lead — follow their gesture.

blocks.heading: Everyday polite formulas
blocks.body: Small words carry a lot of weight in French. "Bonjour" before any request, "s'il vous plaît" and "merci" throughout a conversation, and a proper goodbye all signal respect and warmth, especially with people you don't know well.

examples.french: Bonjour, un café, s'il vous plaît.
examples.english: Hello, a coffee, please.

examples.french: Merci beaucoup, c'est très gentil.
examples.english: Thank you very much, that's very kind.

examples.french: Excusez-moi de vous déranger.
examples.english: Sorry to bother you.

examples.french: Je vous en prie, asseyez-vous.
examples.english: Please, sit down.

examples.french: Au revoir, et bonne journée !
examples.english: Goodbye, and have a good day!

blocks.tip: Skipping "bonjour" before a request can come across as abrupt, even if the rest of your sentence is polite.

blocks.heading: Switching from vous to tu
blocks.body: The verb "tutoyer" means to use "tu" with someone, and "vouvoyer" means to use "vous". The switch usually happens by mutual agreement, often signalled with a simple question.

examples.french: On peut se tutoyer, si tu veux.
examples.english: We can use "tu" with each other, if you like.

examples.french: Je peux vous tutoyer ?
examples.english: May I call you "tu"?

examples.french: Ils se vouvoient encore après dix ans.
examples.english: They still use "vous" with each other after ten years.

examples.french: Ne me vouvoyez pas, on a le même âge !
examples.english: Don't use "vous" with me, we're the same age!

blocks.tip: Both verbs are reflexive when the action is mutual: "se tutoyer", "se vouvoyer".

blocks.heading: Imperative with polite requests
blocks.body: The imperative with "vous" softens naturally when paired with "s'il vous plaît" or a question form. With "tu", the same request feels warmer and more casual, useful once you know someone well.

examples.french: Asseyez-vous, s'il vous plaît.

examples.english: Could you help me?

examples.french: Tu peux m'aider une seconde ?

blocks.tip: "Pourriez-vous...?" (conditional) is the politest way to ask for something in French.

passages.title: Premier jour au bureau
passages.french:
Camille commence un nouveau travail.
Le matin, elle serre la main de son nouveau patron : « Bonjour, madame, enchanté. »
Puis elle rencontre Léa, une collègue de son âge.
— Bonjour, moi c'est Léa. On peut se tutoyer, si tu veux.
— Avec plaisir ! répond Camille, soulagée.
À midi, Léa lui fait la bise avant d'aller déjeuner.
Le soir, Camille dit au revoir à tout le monde.
Elle vouvoie encore son patron, par respect.
Elle rentre chez elle, contente de sa première journée.

Camille starts a new job.
In the morning, she shakes her new boss's hand: "Hello, sir, nice to meet you."
Then she meets Léa, a colleague her own age.

— Gladly! replies Camille, relieved.
At midday, Léa kisses her on the cheek before going to lunch.
In the evening, Camille says goodbye to everyone.
She still uses "vous" with her boss, out of respect.
She goes home, happy with her first day.

lessons.title: Les habitudes françaises
lessons.description: Discover everyday French rhythms: mealtimes, shop hours, and the small customs that shape a normal day.

blocks.heading: Mealtimes: three (or four) fixed moments
blocks.body: In France, meals often happen at fairly set times: breakfast is light, lunch (around noon) is a real meal, and dinner is later in the evening, often after 7:30pm. Many families and children also enjoy "le goûter", an afternoon snack around 4pm.

examples.french: On dîne vers vingt heures chez nous.
examples.english: We have dinner around 8pm at our place.

examples.french: Le déjeuner est le repas principal de la journée.
examples.english: Lunch is the main meal of the day.

examples.french: Les enfants prennent un goûter en rentrant de l'école.
examples.english: Children have a snack when they get home from school.

examples.french: Le petit-déjeuner est souvent léger : pain, café.
examples.english: Breakfast is often light: bread, coffee.

examples.french: On se retrouve à table pour discuter de la journée.
examples.english: We gather at the table to talk about the day.

blocks.tip: Meals are often social moments, not just refuelling stops — expect conversation to take its time.

blocks.heading: Shop hours and the Sunday rhythm
blocks.body: Many small shops close for an hour or two at lunchtime and take a weekly rest day, often Sunday or Monday. Large supermarkets tend to stay open all day, but smaller bakeries and markets follow their own local rhythm.

examples.french: La boulangerie est fermée le lundi.
examples.english: The bakery is closed on Mondays.

examples.french: Le magasin ouvre à neuf heures et ferme à midi.
examples.english: The shop opens at nine and closes at noon.

examples.french: Le dimanche, beaucoup de commerces sont fermés.
examples.english: On Sundays, many businesses are closed.

examples.french: Le supermarché reste ouvert toute la journée.
examples.english: The supermarket stays open all day.

examples.french: Il faut vérifier les horaires d'ouverture avant d'y aller.
examples.english: You should check the opening hours before going.

blocks.tip: If a shop matters to your plans, checking the hours in advance avoids a wasted trip — this rhythm varies a lot by town and season.

blocks.heading: Everyday customs and pace
blocks.body: Daily life in France often includes small, steady habits: a proper lunch break, a slower Sunday, and taking time over a meal rather than rushing. These customs vary from person to person and region to region, but they shape a gentle, familiar rhythm.

examples.french: On prend son temps pour déjeuner.
examples.english: People take their time over lunch.

examples.french: C'est une vieille tradition dans sa famille.
examples.english: It's an old tradition in her family.

examples.french: Chaque région a ses propres coutumes.
examples.english: Every region has its own customs.

examples.french: Le rythme de la semaine change le week-end.
examples.english: The rhythm of the week changes on weekends.

examples.french: Beaucoup de Français font la sieste le dimanche.
examples.english: Many French people take a nap on Sundays.

blocks.tip: These are common patterns, not fixed rules — plenty of French people live at a faster or different pace, especially in big cities.

blocks.heading: Talking about opening hours with ouvrir/fermer
blocks.body: "Ouvrir" (to open) and "fermer" (to close) are regular -ir/-er style verbs often used with times or days. Use "être ouvert/fermé" for a state, and "ouvrir/fermer" for the action itself.

examples.english: The shop opens at nine o'clock.

examples.french: Il est fermé le dimanche.
examples.english: It's closed on Sundays.

examples.french: Elle ferme la boutique à dix-neuf heures.
examples.english: She closes the shop at seven in the evening.

examples.french: Les banques ouvrent tard le samedi.
examples.english: Banks open late on Saturdays.

blocks.tip: "Ouvert" and "fermé" are adjectives after être; "ouvrir" and "fermer" are the action verbs.

blocks.heading: On + reflexive verbs for shared habits
blocks.body: "On" (meaning "we") is very common in spoken French for describing shared, everyday habits, often with reflexive verbs like "se retrouver" or "se reposer".

examples.french: On se retrouve à table le dimanche.
examples.english: We gather at the table on Sundays.

examples.french: On se repose bien pendant les vacances.
examples.english: We rest well during the holidays.

examples.french: On prend son temps le week-end.
examples.english: We take our time on weekends.

examples.french: On partage toujours le dessert.
examples.english: We always share dessert.

blocks.tip: "On" takes a third-person singular verb form, even though it means "we".

Le soir, on dîne assez tard, vers vingt heures, en prenant son temps.

lessons.title: Malentendus culturels
lessons.description: Recognise simple cultural misunderstandings and learn polite, friendly ways to navigate them.

blocks.heading: What is a cultural misunderstanding?
blocks.body: A cultural misunderstanding ("un malentendu culturel") happens when a gesture, word, or habit means something different to two people. It's rarely anyone's fault — it simply comes from different customs. Naming the confusion calmly usually clears it up quickly.

examples.french: C'est un simple malentendu.
examples.english: It's just a simple misunderstanding.

examples.french: Je crois que j'ai mal compris.
examples.english: I think I misunderstood.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas grave, ça arrive.
examples.english: It's not a big deal, it happens.

examples.french: Chaque pays a ses propres habitudes.
examples.english: Every country has its own habits.

examples.french: Il n'y a pas de règle universelle.
examples.english: There's no universal rule.

blocks.tip: Staying curious rather than embarrassed turns a mix-up into a small, friendly learning moment.

blocks.heading: Feeling gêné: what to say
blocks.body: Feeling a little "gêné" (embarrassed or awkward) is completely normal when customs differ — with a greeting, a gift, or the distance people keep while talking. A simple, direct question is often the most polite way through it.

examples.french: Je me sens un peu gêné, excusez-moi.
examples.english: I feel a bit embarrassed, sorry.

examples.french: Je ne suis pas sûr de la règle ici.
examples.english: I'm not sure of the custom here.

examples.french: Est-ce que c'est normal de faire ça ?
examples.english: Is it normal to do that?

examples.french: Dites-moi si je me trompe.
examples.english: Tell me if I'm getting it wrong.

examples.french: J'essaie de m'habituer aux usages d'ici.
examples.english: I'm trying to get used to the customs here.

blocks.tip: Asking a short, direct question usually puts everyone more at ease than guessing silently.

blocks.heading: Explaining and reassuring
blocks.body: When a misunderstanding happens, French speakers often reassure the other person quickly, explain briefly, and move on warmly rather than dwelling on the mistake.

examples.french: Ce n'est vraiment pas grave.
examples.english: It's really not a big deal.

examples.french: Laisse-moi t'expliquer.
examples.english: Let me explain to you.

examples.french: Chez nous, on fait plutôt comme ça.
examples.english: Where we're from, we tend to do it like this.

examples.french: Merci de m'avoir prévenu, je comprends mieux maintenant.
examples.english: Thanks for letting me know, I understand better now.

blocks.heading: Reflexive verbs for feelings and adjustment
blocks.body: Verbs like "se sentir" (to feel), "s'excuser" (to apologise), "s'adapter" (to adapt), and "s'habituer à" (to get used to) are all reflexive — the pronoun changes with the subject.

examples.french: Je me sens un peu gêné.
examples.english: I feel a bit embarrassed.

examples.french: Tu t'habitues vite aux nouvelles règles.
examples.english: You get used to new rules quickly.

examples.french: Il s'excuse pour son erreur.
examples.english: He apologises for his mistake.

examples.french: Nous nous adaptons petit à petit.
examples.english: We're adapting little by little.

blocks.tip: "S'habituer à" is followed by "à" + noun: "s'habituer à la bise", "s'habituer aux horaires".

blocks.heading: Softening statements: ce n'est pas / je crois que
blocks.body: To sound reassuring or less certain, French speakers often soften a statement with "ce n'est pas", "je crois que", or "je ne suis pas sûr(e) que". This is very useful when discussing a misunderstanding calmly.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas grave du tout.
examples.english: It's really not a big deal.

examples.english: I think I misunderstood.

examples.english: I'm not sure that's the rule here.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas une erreur grave.
examples.english: It's not a serious mistake.

blocks.tip: These softening phrases keep the tone friendly, even when pointing out a mix-up.

passages.title: Un petit malentendu
passages.french:
Anna arrive chez la famille Martin pour la première fois.
Madame Martin s'approche pour lui faire la bise, mais Anna tend la main, un peu surprise.
Les deux femmes rient de ce petit malentendu.
— Excusez-moi, dit Anna, je ne savais pas si on se faisait la bise ou pas.
— Ce n'est pas grave du tout ! répond Madame Martin en souriant.
Chaque famille a ses habitudes, ajoute-t-elle.
Plus tard, Anna hésite avant de tutoyer les enfants.
Monsieur Martin la rassure : « Avec eux, tu peux te tutoyer directement. »
Anna se sent vite plus à l'aise, et elle s'habitue rapidement aux petites règles de la maison.
passages.english:
Anna arrives at the Martin family's home for the first time.
Madame Martin approaches to kiss her on the cheek, but Anna holds out her hand, a little surprised.
The two women laugh about this small misunderstanding.
— Sorry, says Anna, I didn't know whether we were doing the cheek kiss or not.
— It's really not a big deal! replies Madame Martin, smiling.
Every family has its own habits, she adds.
Later, Anna hesitates before using "tu" with the children.
Monsieur Martin reassures her: "With them, you can use 'tu' straight away."
Anna quickly feels more at ease, and she gets used to the little house rules fast.
